name: United States Capitol
kicker: Seat of Congress · Iron dome topped by the Statue of Freedom
briefing: In 1793, George Washington laid the cornerstone of a building meant to look like an ancient Roman temple, with rows of columns and a soaring dome. That dome, rebuilt in cast iron by architect Thomas U. Walter, kept rising even as cannons fired during the Civil War. Today the United States Capitol still holds the Senate and the House of Representatives beneath a bronze Statue of Freedom, high above the National Mall.

tossups.p: In 1954, gunshots fired from the visitors’ gallery by Puerto Rican nationalists wounded five members of Congress meeting inside this building. Architect Benjamin Henry Latrobe, who rebuilt this structure after British troops burned it in 1814, also gave some of its columns distinctive corn-cob-shaped capitals.
tossups.r: Decades later, Thomas U. Walter replaced its wood-and-copper dome with one made of cast iron. For 10 points, name this building in Washington, D.C. that houses the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives.

tossups.p: Workers hoisted the final section of a 19.5-foot bronze figure onto this building’s dome in December 1863, an event marked with a 35-gun salute even as the Civil War still raged. That bronze figure, sculpted by Thomas Crawford and cast with help from an enslaved foundry worker named Philip Reid, depicts an allegorical woman called the Statue of Freedom.
tossups.r: She stands atop a dome that was still under construction during the war, meant to show the Union would endure. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building, home to the Senate and House of Representatives.

tossups.p: Italian-born artist Constantino Brumidi [“broo-MEE-dee”] spent years decorating this building’s hallways with paintings of American plants and animals, in corridors that now bear his name. He also painted a fresco inside this building’s dome canopy showing George Washington rising into the heavens between figures representing Liberty and Victory.
tossups.r: That fresco is called _The Apotheosis of Washington_. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building whose cast-iron dome holds Brumidi’s famous ceiling painting.

tossups.p: A curved, dome-shaped ceiling in this building’s old House chamber reflects sound waves so that a whisper on one side of the room can be clearly heard across the floor on the other side. That chamber, now called National Statuary Hall, displays part of a collection of bronze and marble statues, two donated by each state.
tossups.r: Visitors can test the whispering effect by standing on marked spots on the floor. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building that also houses the Senate.

tossups.p: A physician and self-taught architect named William Thornton won an open design competition held in 1792 to create plans for this building, beating out several trained architects. Pierre L’Enfant had already picked a rise called Jenkins’ Hill as the site for this building, reasoning that the high ground made a fitting spot for the nation’s most important structure.
tossups.r: George Washington laid this building’s cornerstone himself in 1793. For 10 points, name this building, home to the Senate and House of Representatives, located in Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: Even though the United States was consumed by civil war, construction continued on this building’s current dome, a decision President Abraham Lincoln defended as proof the Union would go on. Architect Thomas U. Walter designed that dome, made of cast iron instead of stone, to replace an earlier copper-sheathed wooden dome built decades before by Charles Bulfinch.
tossups.r: The finished cast-iron dome weighs almost nine million pounds. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building.

tossups.p: In the 1850s, this building nearly doubled in length when matching wings for an expanding Senate and House were added under the same architect who later designed its dome. At the center of the older part of this building, a circular room called the Rotunda displays large historical paintings, including John Trumbull’s _Declaration of Independence_ and John Gadsby Chapman’s painting of a Virginia woman’s baptism.
tossups.r: That second painting shows Pocahontas kneeling to take the Christian name Rebecca. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building whose Rotunda hosts lying-in-state ceremonies for deceased leaders.

tossups.p: After American forces lost the Battle of Bladensburg in 1814, British troops marched into Washington and set fire to this building, destroying much of the young nation’s library and legislative records. Rebuilding stretched on for years under several different architects before the structure was fully repaired.
tossups.r: That same week, British troops also burned the White House, at the other end of Pennsylvania Avenue. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building, home to the Senate and House of Representatives.

tossups.p: When this building’s wings were expanded in the 1850s to fit a growing Senate and House, architect Thomas U. Walter designed matching new chambers at either end, nearly doubling the structure’s length. He later capped the whole building with a taller dome made of cast iron instead of stone.
tossups.r: That iron dome weighs almost nine million pounds. For 10 points, name this seat of the U.S. Congress in Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: Deceased presidents and other notable Americans have lain in state beneath this building’s dome, inside a circular room ringed with columns and large historical paintings. On bitterly cold inauguration days, presidents have even taken the oath of office inside that same room instead of on the building’s west front.
tossups.r: This room, called the Rotunda, sits at the heart of a building first planned in the 1790s. For 10 points, name this building in Washington, D.C. that houses Congress.

tossups.p: George Washington himself laid the cornerstone of this building in a ceremony in 1793, though he never lived to see it finished. Inside its dome, Italian immigrant artist Constantino Brumidi later painted a swirling fresco showing Washington rising into the heavens between goddesses representing Liberty and Victory.
tossups.r: That ceiling painting is called _The Apotheosis of Washington_. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building where Congress meets.

tossups.p: This building has survived very different kinds of attacks: British troops set it on fire in 1814, and in 1954 gunmen fired into its House chamber from the visitors’ gallery. After the fire, Congress met for several years in a temporary brick building nearby while this one was rebuilt.
tossups.r: Lawmakers still gather here today beneath a dome topped by the Statue of Freedom. For 10 points, name this seat of the U.S. Congress in Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: An enslaved craftsman named Philip Reid helped cast the bronze statue that crowns this building’s dome, working at a foundry outside Washington during the Civil War. Decades earlier, a physician named William Thornton had beaten out professional competitors to design this building’s original layout.
tossups.r: Construction on Thornton’s design began after George Washington laid the cornerstone in 1793. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building.

tossups.p: Hallways inside this building known as the Brumidi Corridors are covered in painted vines, birds, and insects by the same Italian-born artist who decorated the dome’s ceiling. Later artists kept adding new scenes to those corridors long after Brumidi’s death.
tossups.r: His ceiling fresco inside the dome, _The Apotheosis of Washington_, is even more famous. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building.

tossups.p: A bronze statue of a robed woman called Freedom has stood atop this building’s white dome since 1863. Designed in the Neoclassical style, with rows of columns borrowed from ancient Greek and Roman temples, this building sits at the east end of the National Mall in Washington, D.C.
tossups.r: It is home to both the Senate and the House of Representatives. For 10 points, name this seat of the United States Congress.

clues.t: Houses the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives in Washington, D.C.
Famous white dome topped by the bronze Statue of Freedom
Built in the Neoclassical style, with columns modeled on ancient Greek and Roman temples
Cornerstone laid by George Washington in 1793; hilltop site chosen by Pierre L’Enfant
Burned by British troops in 1814 during the War of 1812, the same week as the White House
Circular Rotunda displays large paintings, including Trumbull’s _Declaration of Independence_ and Chapman’s _Baptism of Pocahontas_
National Statuary Hall, the old House chamber, is famous for carrying whispers and displays statues from a collection of two per state
Statue of Freedom was sculpted by Thomas Crawford and cast in bronze with help from Philip Reid, an enslaved foundry worker
Current cast-iron dome, designed by Thomas U. Walter in the 1850s, replaced an earlier wood-and-copper dome by Charles Bulfinch
Original design (1792-93) by Dr. William Thornton, a physician who won an open design competition
Congress first met in the still-unfinished building in November 1800, after the government moved from Philadelphia
Dome construction continued through the Civil War as a sign the Union would endure; the finished iron dome weighs almost 9 million pounds
Architect Benjamin Henry Latrobe, who rebuilt the building after the 1814 fire, also designed columns topped with carved corn-cob capitals
Constantino Brumidi’s fresco _The Apotheosis of Washington_ covers the inside of the dome’s canopy
Statue of Freedom was raised into place in December 1863 with a 35-gun salute during the Civil War
1850s expansion under Thomas U. Walter added the current House and Senate wings, nearly doubling the building’s length
Brumidi Corridors are covered in painted vines, birds, and insects, and later artists kept adding scenes after Brumidi’s death
In 1954, Puerto Rican nationalists fired gunshots from the visitors’ gallery into the House chamber, wounding five lawmakers
Statuary Hall’s whisper effect comes from its curved, dome-shaped ceiling, which focuses sound onto certain floor tiles
Statue of Freedom alone stands about 19.5 feet tall and weighs roughly 15,000 pounds

trap.title: Capitol or White House?
trap.body: The Capitol and the White House were both set on fire by British troops during the same week in August 1814, so a tossup about either building often mentions the other one burning too. Rushing to answer “White House” as soon as you hear “1814” or “burned” can cost you the game if the rest of the clue is actually describing the Capitol.
trap.fix: Listen for the giveaway: “home to the Senate and House of Representatives” or “Congress meets here” means this building. “Where the president lives and works” means the White House.
trap.line: Real answer line: United States Capitol building.
